content.p: Jeffrey Dahmer was convicted on 15 February 1992 of murdering 15 men and boys in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. He had confessed to 17 killings in all, the first in Ohio in 1978. His lawyers argued that he was insane. A jury disagreed after about five hours, and the judge imposed 15 consecutive life sentences. Wisconsin had banned capital punishment in 1853, and life was the sentence. Dahmer lived less than three years longer. On 28 November 1994 another inmate killed him with a metal bar in a prison gymnasium.

The case is remembered for the scale of the killings, but also for how long they went undetected. A man escaped and a boy did not, and the Milwaukee officers who returned that boy to Dahmer's apartment were fired, and a four-week public hearing upheld the firings.
content.h2: An earlier warning, and a light sentence
content.p: Dahmer was not unknown to the courts. In 1988 he was arrested for drugging, fondling and photographing a 13-year-old boy. He pleaded guilty to second-degree sexual assault and to enticing a child, the Chicago Tribune reported. The prosecutor, Gale Shelton, called it "a miracle" that the boy had escaped and asked for a long prison term.

Dahmer's lawyer, Gerald Boyle, asked for leniency, telling the judge, "We don't have a multiple offender here." Dahmer himself pleaded with Circuit Judge William D. Gardner: "please, don't destroy my life." The judge imposed 5 years for the assault and 3 for enticement, then stayed both. Dahmer was ordered to serve a year in a work-release program at the county House of Corrections, which let him keep his job at the Ambrosia Chocolate Co., followed by five years of probation and counselling. He served about 10 months and was released two months early, in March 1990. According to the Tribune, he began killing again two months later, and twelve more people died before his arrest, seven of them in the last four months.
The boy in the 1988 case was Somsack Sinthasomphone, A&E reports. His younger brother Konerak would become one of Dahmer's victims three years later.
content.h2: 27 May 1991: the officers and the boy
content.p: At about 2 a.m. on 27 May 1991, 17-year-old Nicole Childress called 911 from the corner of 25th and State streets in Milwaukee. "He's buck-naked and he has been beaten up," she told the operator. The boy she described was 14-year-old Konerak Sinthasomphone, a Laotian boy whose family had fled Laos in 1980, as The Seattle Times reported. He had been reported missing the day before.

A federal judge's 1993 ruling, quoted by Snopes, records that Dahmer had met Konerak at a shopping mall the previous afternoon and offered to pay him to pose for photographs at his apartment at 924 North 25th Street. While Dahmer went out for beer, the drugged boy got out and into the street. Dahmer came after him and told the young women who had gathered that the boy was a friend who drank too much on weekends. Officers John Balcerzak and Joseph Gabrish arrived, with a second squad arriving minutes later. Dahmer was calm and polite. He gave the officers the name "John Mung", and told them the boy was 18 or 19, or 19 or 20, according to the judge's account. The boy did not answer any questions. Dahmer's own account to police, reported by the Associated Press, was that "John Hmung" was a 20-year-old friend who sometimes stayed with him and often wandered off when drunk.

The young women who had called, Sandra Smith, Tina Spivey and Nicole Childress, say they were rebuffed when they tried to tell the officers what they had seen. The officers walked the boy back to the apartment. They saw photographs of him in bikini briefs, concluded it was a lovers' quarrel, and left. Dahmer later told police that he strangled the boy soon after the officers had gone, and that the body of an earlier victim lay in the bedroom while the officers were there. According to the attorney general's report, the officers smelled a strong odor in the flat and believed it was a bowel movement. A police tape released after the arrest caught an officer saying the "intoxicated Asian naked male" had been "returned to his sober boyfriend", to laughter in the background.

Glenda Cleveland, Childress's aunt and Sandra Smith's mother, telephoned police soon afterwards and was told it was "an intoxicated boyfriend of another boyfriend". "I can't do anything about somebody's sexual preference in life," the officer told her, according to the Seattle Times account of the tape. A Milwaukee Journal Sentinel obituary of Cleveland, quoted by Snopes, says she kept calling after she saw Konerak's picture in a newspaper article about his disappearance, and that five of Dahmer's 17 murders, including Konerak's, came after she tried to alert police.
content.h2: 22 July 1991: the man who got away
content.p: Tracy Edwards, a laborer and roofer, met Dahmer at a neighbourhood mall on 22 July and went to his apartment for a beer. He told The Seattle Times that the flat looked tidy, though a rotten smell and photographs of naked men on the wall struck him. Dahmer, he said, produced handcuffs and a knife and managed to close one cuff on his wrist. "He told me that he was going to kill me and eat my heart out," Edwards said. Edwards said he spent almost five hours talking, drinking and watching the door. At about 11:30 p.m. he punched Dahmer in the face and ran, and flagged down a police car about a block away.

Edwards still wore the handcuff. History reports that the officers at first doubted his story but went back with him. Dahmer told them it was a misunderstanding. Edwards told the Seattle Times that Dahmer stayed calm until police asked for the handcuff key, then tried to stop them when they insisted. The officers noticed Polaroid photographs of dismembered bodies, and Dahmer was arrested. A&E reports that he told the arresting officers, "For what I did, I should be dead."

A&E's account of the apartment search describes human remains, dozens of photographs of victims' bodies and a 57-gallon drum of acid. The Seattle Times, writing in the first days, said at least 11 bodies had been found. In interrogation Dahmer confessed to 17 killings: 16 in Wisconsin and one in Ohio, according to A&E. In the weeks after his arrest, the police officers from the May encounter were suspended and charged with departmental violations. Wisconsin's attorney general, James Doyle, reviewed the incident with more than 40 witness interviews and concluded that the officers showed bad judgement but did not commit a crime, the Associated Press reported.

Dahmer pleaded not guilty to 15 murder counts on 10 September 1991. His first victim, 18-year-old Steven Hicks, had been killed in Ohio in 1978, so that case belonged to Ohio's courts. On 13 January 1992 Dahmer changed his plea to guilty but insane. That removed the need for a trial on the killings and left the jury to decide whether he was legally insane. A&E explains that under Wisconsin's two-stage procedure, only 10 of 12 jurors had to agree for a finding of insanity to stand. A lawyer quoted by A&E said Wisconsin deems a defendant insane who lacked substantial capacity, through mental disease or defect, to appreciate the wrongfulness of his conduct or to conform it to the law.

Testimony began on 30 January 1992 before crowds at the Milwaukee County Courthouse. Boyle told jurors that Dahmer had been obsessed since he was 14 with fantasies and a desire he called necrophilia, a mental disorder, and that it drove the killings. He said his client was "not an evil man," but "a sick man." Prosecutor E. Michael McCann answered that the evidence showed control. Dahmer, McCann said, picked victims who had no car, because an abandoned car would draw police interest, and killed on weekends to leave time to dispose of remains before work on Monday. He also said Dahmer had been in counselling during the months of killing and was "totally uncooperative."

The experts split. Defence witnesses, among them Dr. Judith Becker and Dr. Fred Berlin, described a mental disease. Dr. Park Dietz and Dr. Frederick Fosdal, testifying for the prosecution, said the killings were planned and deliberate; Fosdal quoted Dahmer as saying, "I had choices to make. I made the wrong choices." Court-appointed psychiatrist Dr. George Palermo diagnosed antisocial personality disorder but found no legal insanity. In his closing argument on 14 February, Boyle called his client "a runaway train on a track of madness." McCann showed the jury photographs of the victims and told them, "He's fooled a lot of people," and "Please, please don't let him fool you."
The verdict came on 15 February. A&E says 10 of 12 jurors found that Dahmer was not mentally ill, so the second question never had to be decided. He was guilty.

At sentencing on 17 February, relatives of the dead spoke. According to CBS News, one asked: "Did you ever stop to think that this was someone's son? Did you ever stop to think that this is someone's brother, nephew, uncle, cousin, grandson, or just someone's friend?" Another said, "You almost destroyed me, but I refuse to let you destroy me." The sister of Errol Lindsey, one of the victims, screamed, "Jeffrey, I hate you!"

Dahmer spoke for the first time. "I didn't ever want freedom," he told the court. "Frankly I wanted death for myself." He said he had known he was "sick or evil, or both," and now believed he was sick. He added: "I am prepared for your sentence, which I know will be the maximum." Judge Laurence Gram gave him 15 consecutive life sentences. A&E reports that he was afterwards tried in Ohio for Hicks's killing, found guilty and given another life term; Deseret News later described him as serving 16 consecutive life sentences.

The two officers who had returned Konerak to Dahmer were fired by Police Chief Philip Arreola. After a four-week hearing with 27 witnesses and about 90 hours of testimony, the city's Fire and Police Commission upheld the dismissals in November 1992, the Chicago Tribune reported. In a 52-page report it found that the officers had broken police rules 15 times in a 16-minute investigation. They had not checked Dahmer's record or warrants, verified the boy's name or age, or obtained a medical assessment of his condition, and they had not interviewed the three women who called 911 or acted on Cleveland's information. The commission called the failures gross negligence. One member, Leonard Ziolkowski, dissented, arguing that the men were "real-life patrol officers who exercised bad judgment" who could not have foreseen the outcome.

The department extended recruiting to gay, Asian and other minority communities and expanded cultural-sensitivity training. Snopes reports that the officers were later reinstated with back pay and that the Sinthasomphone family, whose civil-rights suit a judge dismissed in a key part, settled with the Milwaukee Common Council and were paid $850,000. Balcerzak retired in 2017 and Gabrish in 2019, Snopes says.

On 28 November 1994 Dahmer, Christopher Scarver and Jesse Anderson were on a cleaning detail at the prison in Portage, Wisconsin. A criminal complaint described by Deseret News says Scarver hid a 20-inch metal bar from an exercise machine in his trouser leg, found Dahmer alone in a locker room and struck him, then attacked Anderson in a shower room. Scarver told a guard who asked why he was back early, "God told me to do it." Dahmer, 34, died on the way to hospital. Anderson, who was serving a life term for killing his wife, died two days later.

Scarver was already serving a life sentence for murdering Steven Lohman, a man who worked for the Wisconsin Conservation Corps, the agency that had dismissed Scarver; a jury had rejected his insanity plea. Deseret News reported that he had told a psychiatrist he believed he was the son of God. In 2015 Scarver told the New York Post, as quoted by CNN, that he killed Dahmer after confronting him with a newspaper clipping about the crimes and said Dahmer made fake severed limbs out of prison food. History reports that Dahmer survived one attempt on his life in July 1994. CNN says Scarver was sentenced to two life terms for killing Dahmer and Anderson.
